translations.text: Listen! Weary from my journey and sick at heart, I made this song. I gathered from far and wide how those noble men, shining and glorious, showed their courage.

There were twelve of them, famous for their deeds and chosen by the Lord, beloved in their lifetimes. The praise, might and fame of the Prince's thegns spread widely across the earth, a glory that was not small.
The casting of lots guided the holy band to the places where they were to proclaim the Lord's law and explain it to men.
Some of them, Peter and Paul, bold and brave in battle, gave up their lives in Rome through Nero's cruel cunning. Their apostleship is honoured far and wide among the nations of men!
Andrew, too, risked his life in Achaia before Aegeas.

He did not falter before the power of the people's king, or of anyone on earth. Instead he chose for himself eternal and longer-lasting life, light without end, after the battle-hardened man stretched himself on the gallows when the war-play was over, amid the clamour of the crowd.
Listen! We have also heard men learned in the law tell of John's noble life!
As I have heard, that man was dearest to Christ by kinship, in human form, after the King of glory, the source of the angels, the Father of mankind, came to earth through a woman's womb.
He spent all his time teaching the people in Ephesus. From there he set out on his journey along the way of life to the joys of heaven, the bright riches of that dwelling.
His brother James was not slow or reluctant to make that journey either. Among the Jews, before Herod, he had to part with his life by the bite of the sword, his soul parting from his flesh.
Philip was among the people of Asia. From there he quickly reached eternal life through death on the cross, after he was hanged on the gallows in Hierapolis in front of a crowd.
Indeed, it became widely known that the battle-skilled warrior Bartholomew risked his life among the Indians!

Astyages, heathen and blind in mind, ordered him beheaded in Albania because he would not obey the heathen sacrifices or worship idols. The joy of glory and the wealth of life were dearer to him than these false gods.
Thomas likewise boldly ventured into other parts of India. There, through his holy word, the minds of many were enlightened and their hearts strengthened.

Afterwards that bold-spirited man used wondrous power, through the Lord's might, to raise the king's brother in front of the crowds, so that he rose from death, young and brave in battle. His name was Gad. Then Thomas gave up his own life for the people in the conflict.
A sword-stroke from a heathen hand took him. The holy man fell there, wounded in front of the crowds, and from there his soul went to the light of glory as the reward for his victory.

Listen! We have heard from holy books that the truth, the Lord's judgment of God, was revealed among the Ethiopians. The beginning of day dawned, the light of faith, and the land was cleansed by the famous teaching of Matthew.
In anger Hirtacus, the bloodthirsty king, ordered that he be put to death with weapons.
We have heard that James suffered death in Jerusalem before the priests.
The resolute man fell from the stroke of a club, blessed, because of their malice. Now he has eternal life with the King of glory as the reward for his struggle.

Those two warriors, Simon and Thaddeus, brave in battle, were not slow to fight, to the play of shields. Eager for the journey, they went to the land of the Persians. The two of them met their final day together.

Those noble men had to suffer pain through hostile weapons, to win the reward of victory and the true joy, bliss after death, when life was parted from body. They scorned all these passing treasures and empty riches.
So those noble ones, the twelve good-hearted men, met their end. The thanes of glory kept unbroken glory in their minds.
Now I ask any man who loves the course of this song to pray to the holy band for me in my sorrow, asking for peace and help.

Ah, how I will need kind friends on the journey when I must go alone to the long home, the unknown dwelling, and leave behind me my body, my portion of earth, a corpse's spoil, to remain as a comfort for worms.
Here a man wise in forethought, one who delights in songs, can find out who composed this section. ᚠ (F, 'wealth') stands there at the end; noblemen enjoy it on earth.

They cannot be together forever while they dwell in the world. ᚹ (W, 'joy') must fail, and ᚢ (U, 'our' [joy]) in the homeland. Afterwards the borrowed adornments of the body will fall to ruin, just as ᛚ (L, 'water') glides away.
Then ᚳ (C, 'torch') and ᚣ (Y, 'bow') will seek help in the anxious night, and on them lies ᚾ (N, 'need'), the King's service. Now you can know who in these words was made known to men.
Let the man who loves the reciting of this song remember this: that he should ask for help and comfort for me.
I must go far from here, alone, somewhere else. I must look for a dwelling and make a journey out of this world, though I myself do not know where.
The dwellings, the land and the homeland are unknown. So it is for every man, unless he has a share in the divine Spirit.

So let us call more eagerly to God and send our prayers into that bright creation, so that we may enjoy that dwelling, the home on high, where hope is greatest, where the King of angels gives the pure a never-ending reward.
Now his praise stands forever, great and glorious, and his might lasts over all creation, eternal and always young.
